title: The Empty Fort Strategy: Was Sima Yi Even There That Day?
description:
Jieting has just been lost. In the novel, Zhuge Liang sits on the wall of Xicheng burning incense and playing the qin, all four gates wide open, and Sima Yi's 150,000 troops reach the walls and then pull back. Everyone has heard this scene, yet the main text of Chen Shou's Records of the Three Kingdoms does not have a single word of it.

This episode peels the story back layer by layer, in the order the records turn up: the version Guo Chong told at the court of the Prince of Fufeng in the early Western Jin (Yangping, 10,000 against 200,000, flags lowered, drums silenced, no qin); Pei Songzhi refuting it point by point in his commentary two centuries later, ending with "so we know everything this book cites is false"; then Sima Yi's real months in the Book of Jin: stationed at Wan, reaching Xincheng in eight days to strike Meng Da, then back to Wan; Cao Zhen and Zhang He, who really faced Zhuge Liang in 228 AD; and the moment on the day of the defeat at Jieting when Wang Ping's 1,000 men beat their drums and Zhang He, "suspecting an ambush", did not dare pursue. The qin, the city wall, Sima Zhao's question, Xicheng and Jieting are all absent from Guo Chong's version; they only appear later, in chapter 95 of the novel Romance of the Three Kingdoms.

Quotations from the official histories follow transcriptions of the Wenyuange Siku Quanshu edition of the Records of the Three Kingdoms (with Pei Songzhi's commentary) and the Book of Jin; the novel follows the 120-chapter edition on Project Gutenberg. The source of every quotation, year and number is listed in the references below; sentences that begin "we think" are this channel's view.

The illustrations in this episode are AI-generated. The historical figures are cartoon characters, unnamed and not meant to resemble anyone.

kc101.text: Jieting just fell. The novel's Zhuge Liang is at Xicheng for grain.

kc102.text: Suddenly, word comes: Sima Yi is coming with 150,000 men, and the town has just 2,500.

kc103.text: He opens the gates, has troops sweep, dressed as folk;

kc104.text: then sits on the wall, burns incense, plays qin.

kc105.text: Sima Zhao asks his father: is he faking, with no men?

kc106.text: Sima Yi: Zhuge Liang is always cautious. It's an ambush. Retreat!

kc107.text: The army withdraws. Later, even the novel's Zhuge Liang laughs:

kc108.text: Were I Sima Yi, I'd not retreat.

kc110.text: Was the qin in the earliest version?

kc111.text: The first man to tell it told it to Sima Yi's own son.

kc112.text: That year, someone else below a hill kept beating a drum. And who was he trying to fool?

kc113.text: On the day of the Empty Fort, where was Sima Yi?

kc201.text: But in the main text of Chen Shou's Records of the Three Kingdoms, there isn't a word of it.

kc202.text: The first empty-fort story hides in a later commentary on the text.

kc203.text: Decades on, in early Western Jin, Sima Jun, Prince of Fufeng, held Guanzhong.

kc204.text: He's the son from the opening: Sima Yi's.

kc205.text: His officials talked of Zhuge Liang, mostly mocking: so little strength, such big plans.

kc206.text: But one guest, Guo Chong from Jincheng, stood up for Zhuge Liang.

kc207.text: He said Zhuge Liang did five things the world never knew.

kc208.text: The empty fort was the third.

kc209.text: Guo Chong sets it not in Xicheng but Yangping, Hanzhong.

kc210.text: Zhuge Liang sends Wei Yan east with the main army, keeping just 10,000.

kc211.text: Sima Yi comes with 200,000, just missing Wei Yan, and closes to sixty li away.

kc212.text: Too late to catch Wei Yan now; the officers all turn pale.

kc213.text: So what does Zhuge Liang do?

kc214.text: He stays calm: flags lowered, drums silenced, and no one may leave the tents.

kc215.text: Then he opens all four gates, sweeps, and sprinkles water.

kc216.text: Sima Yi always found Zhuge Liang steady; seeing him act weak, he grows suspicious.

kc217.text: He suspects an ambush, almost the novel's line: “It must be an ambush.”

kc218.text: So he leads his army off to the northern hills.

kc219.text: Next morning at breakfast, Zhuge Liang claps and laughs to his staff:

kc220.text: Sima Yi must think I'm timid, with an ambush; so, the hills.

kc221.text: The scouts come back: just so.

kc222.text: Guo Chong: Sima Yi later learned, and fumed.

kc223.text: But was Sima Yi ever actually bluffed into retreat by Zhuge Liang?

kc224.text: And the qin? Guo Chong's version has no qin, no city wall, no Sima Zhao.

kc226.text: All that only shows up in the later novel.

kc227.text: That year Zhuge Liang really was around Yangping; Chen Shou says so.

kc228.text: And the Sima Yi outside the walls? Was he really there that year?

kc301.text: The checker was Pei Songzhi, who annotated the Records.

kc302.text: He presented his commentary to the emperor in 429 AD, some two centuries after the battle.

kc303.text: His rule: if it doesn't add up, correct it.

kc304.text: Before the five things, he writes: of course I'd love good Zhuge stories.

kc305.text: And then he writes: what Guo Chong says is all highly doubtful.

kc306.text: First he checks Guo Chong's Yangping.

kc307.text: When Zhuge Liang first reached Yangping, Sima Yi led Jingzhou, based at Wan.

kc308.text: He adds: only after a certain man died did Sima Yi face Zhuge in Guanzhong.

kc310.text: He checks the records: Wei did once send Sima Yi from Wan, by way of Xicheng, to attack Shu.

kc311.text: Xicheng? The same place as the town in the novel?

kc312.text: Pei's point: around then, there was no fighting at Yangping.

kc313.text: He counts troops: remember Guo Chong's 200,000? So many men, who knew the town was thinly held.

kc314.text: Even fearing an ambush, they'd make camp and go slowly. Why turn and leave?

kc315.text: Remember the novel's Zhuge: “Were I Sima Yi, I'd not retreat”?

kc316.text: Pei Songzhi's math says exactly the same.

kc317.text: Pei also checked Wei Yan, sent east with the army.

kc318.text: Wei Yan kept asking for 10,000 men on another route; Zhuge always refused.

kc319.text: He wouldn't give him even that. Why hand him the army and keep weak troops?

kc320.text: Last, he looks at who was listening to this story.

kc321.text: Remember the Prince of Fufeng up front? Guo Chong told his father's shame.

kc322.text: Pei says: telling a son his father's faults is unthinkable.

kc323.text: Yet the book says the prince loved it.

kc324.text: So his verdict: everything this book cites is false.

kc325.text: But that's only Pei Songzhi's word. Where was Sima Yi that year? Do the other histories agree?

kc401.text: They do. The Book of Jin says that from June 227 AD, he was posted to that very same town of Wan.

kc402.text: The troops of Jing and Yu were his.

kc403.text: Late that year, Meng Da of Xincheng rebelled.

kc404.text: Meng Da figured in a letter: Wan was 800 li from Luoyang, 1,200 from him.

kc406.text: He marched day and night: eight days.

kc407.text: Wu and Shu sent aid; Sima Yi sent officers to block it.

kc408.text: After sixteen days, the town fell. Meng Da died.

kc409.text: Then he led his troops back to Wan.

kc410.text: Remember the opening question? On the Empty Fort day, where was Sima Yi?

kc411.text: The histories put both in the same month: January 228 AD, Xincheng fell;

kc413.text: That spring, Zhuge Liang feigned another route and led his army to Qishan.

kc415.text: Grand General Cao Zhen held Guanyou; Zhang He was sent to Jieting.

kc416.text: Sima Yi isn't on this list.

kc417.text: And Sima Zhao, who asked his father? He was about 18; no history says he went on campaign.

kc418.text: Ma Su led Shu's men at Jieting.

kc419.text: Ignoring Zhuge Liang's plan, he left the water for a hill.

kc420.text: Wang Ping warned him; no use.

kc421.text: No water up there. How long?

kc422.text: Zhang He arrived and cut their water path.

kc501.text: Their leader: Wang Ping, who'd warned Ma Su.

kc502.text: The drums kept on; the ranks held.

kc503.text: Zhang He arrived and halted. Suspecting an ambush, he held back.

kc504.text: Remember the man drumming below the hill? Wang Ping. The one fooled was Zhang He.

kc505.text: Thus Wang Ping rallied the stragglers, led them back.

kc506.text: And the victor, Zhang He? Where did he go?

kc507.text: He was sent to Jingzhou, under Sima Yi.

kc508.text: What was Sima Yi doing that winter? Building a navy in Jingzhou to sail down and hit Wu.

kc509.text: But winter water was low, big ships stuck; Zhang He withdrew.

kc511.text: In 230 AD, Sima Yi really set out from Xicheng, cutting roads.

kc512.text: Zhuge Liang waited at Chiban, Chenggu.

kc513.text: Then it rained 30-plus days, the plank roads broke; Wei pulled back.

kc514.text: That Xicheng is on the upper Han, not the novel's Xicheng.

kc515.text: Pei said they'd only face off after a man died. Who was he?

kc516.text: Cao Zhen. In 231 AD, Cao Zhen died of illness; Sima Yi moved west from Jingzhou.

kc517.text: That year Zhuge besieged Qishan; Sima Yi attacked him.

kc519.text: Back to the question: was Sima Yi ever bluffed back by Zhuge Liang?

kc520.text: Three years later, Zhuge Liang died in camp.

kc521.text: After his death, Shu turned its banners and drummed, as if to charge Sima Yi.

kc522.text: And Sima Yi pulled back, not daring to close in.

kc523.text: People said: “Dead Zhuge sends living Zhongda running.” Zhongda was Sima Yi.

kc524.text: Sima Yi said: I can foresee the living, not the dead.

kc525.text: Remember that list? Whether by Guo Chong or the novel, the man facing Zhuge Liang that year wasn't Sima Yi.

kc526.text: We think what really fooled the enemy that year wasn't a qin on a wall, but that drum below Jieting's hill.

kc528.text: Where'd you first see the Empty Fort: book, stage, TV?

kc529.text: We cover only what's in the records. Subscribe to open files with us.
